### United Nations E/CN.9/2024/2

Economic and Social Council Distr.: General 21 February 2024 Original: English

Advance unedited version

Commission on Population and Development 
Fifty-seventh session 
29 April 2024 to 03 May 2024 
Item 3 (b) of the provisional agenda* 
General debate 

Assessing the status of implementation of the Programme of Action of the International Conference on Population and Development and its contribution to the follow-up and review of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development during the decade of action and delivery for sustainable development Report of the Secretary-General

Summary

During the three decades since the International Conference on Population and Development, held in Cairo, Egypt, in 1994, the world’s population has grown by nearly 2.5 billion and is expected to increase by another 1.7 billion over the next 30 years. Rapid population growth continues to be a challenge for a subset of developing countries with persistent high levels of fertility. Such countries often lack sufficient resources to invest in health, education and decent employment and to move towards sustainable economic systems powered by clean energy. Like other countries, they are undergoing a demographic transition towards longer lives and smaller families but are at a relatively early stage. As the fertility level continues to fall, these countries can benefit from an opportunity for accelerated economic growth and development known as the demographic dividend. For most other countries, population growth has slowed down, and an increasing number are now experiencing population decline and advanced levels of population ageing. The rapid growth of the older population highlights the need to invest in lifelong learning, to create age-friendly work environments, to expand flexible, including part-time, employment options for older persons, and to develop sustainable long-term care and social protection systems to address the needs of the population throughout the life course. Over the next 30 years, an increasingly interdependent world will require expanded international cooperation to mitigate anthropogenic climate change and environmental degradation, to facilitate safe, orderly and regular migration, and to advance the planning and implementation of national policies, including for the promotion of sustainable urbanization, as cities will be the home of around two thirds of the world’s population by 2050. ________________ * E/CN.9/2024/1.

## I. Population megatrends since 1994 and prospects until 2054

1. Since the convening of the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD) 
in 1994, the world has experienced major transformations. The global population, which stood at 
5.6 billion in 1994, grew to 8.1 billion in 2024, with projections indicating a further increase to 
nearly 9.9 billion in 2054. Much of this growth will be driven by the momentum generated by past 
growth, which shifts the population towards younger ages and ensures the continued growth of the 
population in the reproductive ages over the next few decades, even after the number of births per 
women falls to much lower levels. 
2. Population growth rates vary greatly by region. Sub-Saharan Africa is expected to contribute 
over half of the global population increase until 2050 due to sustained high levels of fertility. In the 
other regions, the rate of population growth is mostly positive but declining. Eastern and South 
Eastern Asia, and Europe and Northern America will begin to experience population decline before 
2050, with Latin America and the Caribbean following shortly thereafter. By 2050, most of the 
increase in global population will be contributed by three regions—sub-Saharan Africa, Northern 
Africa and Western Asia, and Central and Southern Asia. 
3. Fertility has continued to decline since 1994. High-fertility countries have become concentrated 
in sub-Saharan Africa, while regions like Eastern and South-Eastern Asia have witnessed significant 
reductions due to socioeconomic development and improved access to family planning. 
4. Life expectancy at birth has seen remarkable improvements, rising globally from 64.5 years in 
1994 to 73.7 years for both sexes in 2024, driven by reductions in mortality rates across the age 
range. Improvements in survivorship, coupled with falling fertility, have transformed the age 
distribution of the global population. The number of children under age five globally has remained 
stable, while the number of persons aged 65 or over has more than doubled over the past 30 years 
and is expected to double again by 2054. 
5. The world’s population is also increasingly urban, with nearly 58 per cent of the global 
population residing in urban areas in 2024. The rural population, living mostly in developing 
countries, is expected to continue to decline over the coming decades. 
6. International migration has also intensified. An estimated 281 million people were living 
outside their country of birth in 2020, a substantial increase from 161 million in 1995. Europe hosts 
the largest number of international migrants, followed by Northern America and then by Northern 
Africa and Western Asia. 
Global convergence in demographic trends since 1994 
7. Since the 1994 Cairo conference, there have been widespread reductions in mortality and 
fertility rates across countries and regions. Nevertheless, large disparities remain, . For fertility, the 
global decline (figure I) has been driven by significant reductions in lower-middle-income countries 
(LMICs) and low-income countries (LICs), which have moved closer to levels observed in high 
income countries (HICs).

8. Adolescent fertility rates have also decreased globally, narrowing the gap between LICs and 
HICs. However, considerable differences persist within income groups, indicating the need for 
targeted interventions. 
9. Life expectancy has risen globally, with a narrowing gap between LICs and HICs (figure II). 
Despite improvements, today over 60 countries still fall below the ICPD target of a life expectancy 
at birth of 70 years. Mortality rates, including for under-five mortality and maternal mortality, have 
declined across all income groups. Nevertheless, achieving the SDG target for child mortality 
remains a challenge for many LICs and LMICs.

10. Population growth rates have not exhibited a comparable convergence across income groups. While there has been some convergence between HICs and upper-middle-income countries (UMICs), the gap between HICs and LICs persists. Projections suggest this gap may only slightly narrow over the next 30 years. 11. The demographic transition towards longer lives and smaller families has led to a rapid upward shift in the population age distribution, especially in HICs and UMICs, while LICs still maintain youthful age structures. A net inflow of international migrants to HICs has helped to sustain positive rates of population growth, countering a near-zero or negative balance of births over deaths.

## II. Regional perspectives on population and development

Economic Commission for Africa (ECA) 
12. The regional review held in 2023 emphasized the significance of the ICPD Programme of 
Action in the context of the 2030 Agenda and the African Union’s 2063 Agenda. The review 
acknowledges that, despite political commitment and increased involvement of stakeholders, the 
implementation of population policies in Africa has been limited due to economic shocks and 
setbacks, which have constrained the fiscal space. 
13. Although African nations made significant progress in reducing extreme poverty in recent 
decades, the COVID-19 pandemic reversed some of those gains, pushing millions into poverty. 
Today, the continent accounts for 80 per cent of the world’s poor. 
14. With a population of 1.4 billion, Africa is the world’s second-most populous region. It is 
projected to contribute over half of the global population increase between now and 2050. 
15. The anticipated ageing of the currently youthful population (median age below 20 years) 
requires investments in human capital to build a productive workforce. Sustained reductions in the 
fertility rate present the potential for a demographic dividend, if the population has access to quality 
health care, education and decent work. 
16. Africa continues to experience gains in life expectancy, and both the number and the share of 
persons aged 65 years or over are projected to increase in the future. While increased longevity is a 
positive outcome of human development, it also brings challenges related to the rising costs of health 
care and old-age pensions. Africa has the lowest coverage of social protection globally, with only 
17 per cent of the population receiving at least one social protection benefit. 
17. The continent is also undergoing significant changes in spatial population distribution due to 
migration and urbanization, with the proportion urban expected to reach 59 per cent by 2050. 
Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) 
18. The 2023 regional review of the ICPD Programme of Action highlighted three thematic 
priorities: (a) population dynamics and sustainable development; (b) families and sexual and 
reproductive health over the life course; and (c) inequalities, social inclusion and rights. With a 
population of 1.3 billion in 2023, the region has grown by 160 million since 1994; a further increase 
of 40 million is expected by 2050. 
19. While population dynamics vary across countries, the region is characterized by low levels of 
fertility and ageing populations. With a regional average of 1.7 births per woman, the total fertility 
rate lies below the replacement level for most countries. 
20. People aged 65 years or over account for 17.6 per cent of the region’s population. One in three 
countries in the region have experienced population decline since 1994, and half are projected to do 
so by 2030. 
21. Immigration partially offsets the impacts of low fertility in Western Europe and North America, 
propping up the population growth rate and attenuating the process of population ageing. However, 
a net outflow of international migrants exacerbates population ageing and contributes to population 
decline in Eastern and South-Eastern Europe. 

5/19

22. While the region has seen substantial progress towards most ICPD objectives, gains have been 
uneven within and across countries, and some recent crises have disrupted favourable trends. 
Overall, people in the region are living longer, healthier lives, yet progress towards universal health 
coverage has recently slowed. Disparities by sub-region, gender and age persist in deaths caused by 
non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and suicide. Premature mortality rates from NCDs are below 
175 per 100,000 population in several Northern European countries, but they exceed 550 per 
100,000 in parts of Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Suicide mortality rates among people aged 65 
or over are twice as high as for the rest of the population. Access to quality education, lifelong 
learning, and decent work is improving, but persons with disabilities, youth and older persons still 
lag behind. Progress in reducing poverty and social exclusion has also slowed.
